title: Papers with open peer-review reports are less likely to be retracted | Nature

title: arXiv welcomes inaugural CEO and founding Board of Directors
content: "We have exciting news to share today: the appointment of Dr. Penelope Lewis as arXiv’s inaugural Chief Executive Officer and the establishment of our Board of Directors. If you’ve been following arXiv’s transition to an independent nonprofit organization, these leadership appointments mark a significant step in our journey. Having a CEO and Board in place strengthens our governance, sustainability, and capacity to serve the global research community for generations to come. For more than three decades, arXiv has enabled rapid and open sharing of scientific research. It has operated largely on the support and dedication of its staff, moderators, volunteers, members, funders, and, for the past 25 years, the institutional backing of Cornell. As the scale, reach, and importance of the platform have grown, so too has the need for more formal leadership and governance structures that support long-term sustainability. The appointment of the first CEO and creation of an international governing board reflect our commitment to maintaining arXiv as a trusted, community-centered resource while preparing for future opportunities and evolution. title: NIH Director Bhattacharya kills more health disparities grants | Science | AAAS
content:
"Now, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya is ending two more grants, both for health disparities research at the University of Pittsburgh (Pitt).

A 4 August letter sent by Bhattacharya to Pitt’s research office informing it that a grant to social epidemiologist Tamara Dubowitz “will be terminated in full” confirms that more cancellations are coming...Her 5-year, NIH-funded study exploring health and socioeconomic factors contributing to cognitive aging and Alzheimer’s in African Americans living in poor neighborhoods in Pittsburgh is nearing completion, and her team has already spent $7 million of the $9.6 million grant. She says neither her project nor the other Pitt grant slated to be killed were given a chance to adjust their research to comply with new NIH priorities Bhattacharya has detailed."

title: Choosing What’s Next: Introducing the National Open Education Priorities Process — Open Education Association
content: "Open education is more relevant to the problems facing higher education than ever before, yet it is too often absent from the rooms where decisions are made. Twenty years of OER advocacy successfully made the case against expensive textbooks. That case still holds, but it no longer opens every door it used to. This fall, the Open Education Association invites the open education field to collaborate on a process to choose national priorities: specific problems that higher education leaders and policymakers are already trying to solve, where open education offers a solution. Examples could include how to train nurses faster by reducing cost as a barrier, how to break down silos in educational data, or how to improve AI literacy through open materials. Working collaboratively across the field, this process will surface a list of potential priorities, discuss them throughout the fall, and select the final priorities at a national summit in November. This webinar will officially kick off the process and explain how it will work, including what we mean by national priorities, how to join or host a listening session, and how to apply to serve as a representative at a national summit this

title: NOT-OD-26-100: Implementation Update: NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan Requirements
content: "This Guide Notice provides an update to the research community on forms changes when NIH transitions to the updated Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plan format which includes reporting changes to previously approved DMS Plans. Background The NIH Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Policy ensures that the benefits of taxpayer funded research are maximally shared to advance research, improve health outcomes, and cultivate trust in the biomedical research enterprise. When released in 2023, NIH issued supplemental information outlining desired elements of a DMS Plan. After several years of implementation experience, NIH issued Notice NOT-OD-26-046, Updated Elements of an NIH Data Management and Sharing Plan, to provide a structured template and format across all NIH Institutes, Centers, and Offices (ICOs.) NIH is finalizing implementation of this new format to ensure NIH's data sharing goals are achieved while reducing administrative burden and improving reporting efficiency. The planned updates to the DMS Plan format do not constitute a change in NIH policy. content:
"Repositories are key institutional tools that ensure access to and reuse of valuable research outputs. To better support those goals, some institutions have developed or use shared repository services. USRN is bringing together a panel to discuss their use cases and experiences of shared repository services.

Panelists will share how the conversations about shared repository services started and evolved at their institution, who was involved, and what services are now being utilized. This conversation aims to share the experiences of those using shared repositories services (without digging into the technical implementation) and to gauge interest in the topic for future conversations."

title: [2607.00546v1] Open Science in Astrophysics: Citation Benefits of Open Code, Open Data, and Open Access
content: Abstract: We analyze the relationship between open-accessibility in data, code, and paper text in astrophysics using a sample of 53,194 peer reviewed papers published between January 2021 and April 2025, drawn from NASA's Astrophysics Data System (ADS). We measure eleven quantities: open accessibility of text, open-code status, open-data status, number of grants received, code size, programming language, data repository size, citation count, number of authors, paper length, and publication date. We break down citation advantages based on six astrophysical sub-fields: Solar System, Planet, Stellar, ISM, High Energy, and Galaxies+Cosmology, determined by keywords. This is accomplished by tuning a multivariate least-squares regression model with alongside partial correlations and non-parametric tests to isolate the contribution of each facet of openness. After controlling for the aforementioned quantities, we find significant citation advantages associated with all three forms of openness: open data (+32%, p < 10^-24), open access (+26%, p < 10^-67), and open code (+16%, p = 0.003). The open-data citation advantage is present in all six sub-fields, and especially in Galaxies+Cosmology

title: How collective funding supports sustainable publishing
content:
"Diamond open access is defined by UNESCO as ‘an equitable scholarly publishing model, supported by shared infrastructures and open licensing, providing scholarly knowledge as a digital public good with no fees for readers or authors.’ One increasingly important approach to funding this form of open access is collective funding, which allows libraries to directly support publishers and publishing infrastructure, making it possible to publish without the need for article or book publication charges. 

As members of initiatives such as the Open Book Collective (OBC) and Open Journals Collective (OJC), who have both recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding, and with a Jisc-supported scheme for our journals programme, LSE Press is part of this wider movement that seeks to establish more equitable, sustainable, community-governed alternatives for open access publishing. Together, OBC and Jisc membership has already brought us support from 29 libraries across the UK, Europe and North America."

title: Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI): A Community-Driven Strategic Plan, 2027 – 2030 | Zenodo
content: Abstract: Federally funded research data is a public good, but the repositories and infrastructure that keep it findable, accessible, and usable have long been fragile — a fragility that recent funding, staffing, and policy disruptions have laid bare. Because the research data system is highly distributed, spanning thousands of repositories and practitioners across many domains, no single organization can address these vulnerabilities alone. This document is the draft strategic plan for the Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI), a proposed cross-sectoral coalition working to build a more resilient ecosystem for federally funded research data. It sets out the case for action, a shared vision and guiding principles, and three strategic pillars: assessing and monitoring the repository landscape; developing diverse, sustained funding and governance; and building a shared outreach, advocacy, and action strategy. It also includes a starting point for coalition governance and an outline of next steps toward implementation. title: How preprints accelerate the time to first citation of the subsequent journal articles? | Scientometrics | Springer Nature Link
content: Abstract: This study examines whether journal articles with preprints are cited more rapidly than those without preprints. We construct a matched sample of articles published in the same journal, year, volume, and issue to ensure comparability between articles with and without preprints. Survival analysis is employed to estimate the temporal advantage of articles with preprints in receiving the first citation relative to those without preprints, while OLS regression quantifies this advantage in terms of days. The key findings are as follows: (1) articles with preprints have a 35.2% higher hazard of receiving their first citation than those without preprints; (2) among articles that received at least one citation during the observation period, articles with preprints were associated with a 69.042-day shorter time to first citation than comparable articles without preprints; (3) both early visibility and the additional dissemination channels of preprint platforms are associated with a shorter time to first citation, with early visibility showing a relatively stronger association. title: Utilization of Institutional Repositories among Users in Selected Universities in Karnataka: An Empirical Study
content: Abstract: The present study examines the utilization of Institutional Repositories among users in selected universities in Karnataka. The study is based on primary data collected through a structured questionnaire from teaching faculty and research scholars. The findings revealed that a large proportion of respondents (87.16%) were aware of Institutional Repositories, and a majority (75.31%) actively used them for academic and research purposes. Institutional Repositories were primarily utilized for accessing research-related materials and supporting scholarly activities. The study further indicated that users perceived several benefits, including enhanced accessibility and visibility of scholarly work, increased citation impact, and long-term preservation of institutional outputs. However, respondents also reported challenges such as technical issues, poor browsing ability, limited access to repository resources, and lack of institutional support, which affected effective utilization. title: [2607.25220v1] Preprints Without Curation Are Increasingly Cited by Journals
content: Abstract: The recent strain on peer review systems necessitates the publish-review-curate model, where the public dissemination of manuscripts is decoupled from formal peer review and later editorial processes. Citation norms traditionally pointed to the curated version; those that subsequently appear in peer-reviewed journals. Citations to preprints are therefore generally expected to occur only to those eventually curated. Using metadata from six major preprint servers linked to the world's largest bibliographic reference database, and focusing on citations from long-established journals with rigorous editorial workflows, we compare observed citation rates with a null model reflecting the expected rate if authors were indifferent between preprints and journal articles. The growth is evident in both citation intensity and the breadth of adoption: at its peak in 2021, nearly one in five journal articles cited at least one preprint. The preference to cite preprints has grown exponentially since the mid-2010s, with key inflection points coinciding with the launch of bioRxiv (2013) and the introduction of a preprint content type in Crossref's DOI system (2016). title: Openness and Inequity in Scientific Research
content: "This special issue examines the promises and limitations of Open Science (OS) and the conditions that produce inequity, injustice, and exclusion in research. Going well beyond the free sharing of publications typically referred to as Open Access, OS aspires to take advantage of new communication technologies to enhance access to and use of all the components of research, ranging from data to models, software, techniques, instruments, protocols and review procedures (Boulton and Royal Society Citation2012). OS advocates argue that the competitive and proprietary regimes and metrics under which research is currently conducted damage the reliability, quality, and social relevance of science. The main reason is that these regimes and metrics erode opportunities for critical scrutiny and collaboration which are the hallmarks of scientific work. They also disincentivise the exchange of insights and methods within and across disciplines (Radder Citation2010) leading to an inward-looking academic culture more interested in competing for the next high-impact publication than in developing reliable long-term solutions to societal and environmental challenges (Edwards and Roy Citation2017).

title: The Diamond road to Open Science | Swiss Medical Weekly
content: Abstract: Diamond Open Access is the fairest and most sustainable model for scientific communication. The Diamond model promotes editorial independence, supports researchers by waiving article processing charges, and serves as an indispensable public research infrastructure. “Read & Publish” agreements increase dependence on large commercial publishers, and some of the funds currently spent on such agreements could instead be used to provide long-term support for Diamond journals. Promising models for sustainable funding and collaboration are emerging through national and international initiatives. However, Switzerland is already providing concrete evidence that institutions do not have to wait until national mechanisms are fully developed. In 2025, the University of Lausanne launched the “Diamond Open Access Fund”, a pioneering initiative of its kind in Switzerland. The future development of Diamond Open Access should focus not only on sustainable funding but also on enhancing the quality, transparency, and culture of scholarly publishing. content: Abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to explore the motivations and experiences of university academics who engage in open access publishing for survival and academic development. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multiple-case qualitative approach, drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of practice to investigate the activities and experiences of seven academics as they strived to publish in indexed open access journals. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and observation, focusing on the academics’ strategies for obtaining cultural capital. title: OA or Nonchalant: A Survey of Open Access Dissemination Initiatives of Higher Education Institution Library Websites and Systems in the Philippines | Balbin | College & Research Libraries
content: Abstract: The objective of this study is to determine the extent to which libraries are disseminating open access (OA) through conducting a survey of the different library websites and systems of higher education institution (HEI) libraries in the Philippines. This also aims to identify the types, subject fields, quantity, and quality of the OA resources shared by private and public HEI libraries in terms of the links they embed in their websites and systems. The study employed a quantitative research design focusing on website analysis. The findings revealed that many libraries have established websites and systems that they use to embed information about OA resources. Most OA resource links disseminated by HEI libraries are multidisciplinary, and the majority of these are OA journals. Comparing the number of OA resources advertised by HEI libraries, private institutions tend to share more links. From the 2,917 OA resources embedded in 312 library websites, the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) topped the most shared OA resource.

title: Not Just Monetary: Arts and Humanities Scholars’ Perspectives on the Costs of Open Access Publishing | Skaggs | College & Research Libraries
content: Abstract: Bibliometric and survey-based studies have documented different open access (OA) publishing practices among scholars across academic disciplines. This article reports on interviews conducted with arts and humanities scholars from the United States, and it explores how OA intersects with their research and publication practices. Beyond the considerable financial costs of OA publishing, findings demonstrate that arts and humanities scholars contend with opportunity, reputational, equity, and time costs as they consider and engage with OA publishing. The authors discuss the implications of these costs for librarians who facilitate the dissemination, discovery, and preservation of arts and humanities scholarship.

title: Moving Beyond the Publisher Playbook: Why State-Level Contract Law is Essential to the Future of Digital Library Rights | Library Journal
content:
"In his recent piece in Library Journal, Alan S. Inouye characterizes the last 15 years of library digital book advocacy as well-intentioned “firefighting” and incrementalism, calling instead for a retreat from state-level legislative action in favor of a vague, long-term national strategy. While a retrospective on the digital lending landscape is welcome, Inouye’s analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current legal architecture driving the library ebook movement today. And, in several critical respects, it recycles the very talking points of the publisher lobby it purports to analyze objectively....

To properly address the future of library digital books, three things require immediate correction: the piece’s misleading framing, its foundational legal errors, and its uncritical repetition of publisher talking points, which have been soundly rejected by caselaw, legislators, lawyers, and librarians across every state where ebook bills have become law or are currently advancing...."

title: Financing Open Research: a Focus on African Publishing Platforms and Journals | INASP
content: "Africa's open access publishing ecosystem, spanning roughly 1,790 journals and platforms like AJOL, AfricaArXiv, and Open Research Africa, is far more fragile than its policy visibility suggests. A new INASP policy paper reveals that most of this infrastructure survives through unpaid academic labour, informal institutional subsidies, and short-term donor cycles rather than any coordinated public investment. The total cost of sustaining the entire system is estimated at $7.2 to $14.3 million annually, a figure modest by global standards, yet no structured financing mechanism exists to cover it. The core argument is not that Africa lacks resources for open research, but that existing contributions are unrecognised, uncoordinated, and unsustainable in their current form. The paper calls for Science Granting Councils, national governments, universities, and regional bodies to formalise institutional underwriting, integrate publishing infrastructure into national research budgets, and build regional consortia."

title: Announcing the Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI) Strategic Plan
content: "Since Fall 2025, the Center for Open Science (COS) has been working with a committee of experts in research data infrastructures to develop a strategic plan for the Coalition for Resilient Research Data Infrastructure (CRRDI) — a nascent cross-sectoral coalition working to build a more resilient ecosystem for federally funded research data. Today, we are releasing that draft plan for community comment by September 30, 2026. This effort began with a grant from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation to respond to growing concerns about the integrity and resilience of public data. As a champion of lifecycle open science, COS is committed to persistent and reliable public access to research information — and long attuned to how fragile the infrastructure supporting that access can be. We recognized, however, that we are one of many actors in a complex, distributed, and interconnected research information ecosystem, and that no single organization can advance a more resilient future for research data infrastructure alone. title: EXCLUSIVE – Amy Brand: Publishing for a new era - Research Information
content: "MIT Press has a well-earned reputation as one of the sector’s most innovative university presses. Whether through Direct to Open, experiments with digital textbooks or new approaches to open scholarship, innovation has become a defining characteristic of the organisation. But Amy rejects the idea that innovation is a luxury enabled by financial security. In fact, she argues precisely the opposite. For university presses, whose financial margins are often tighter than their commercial counterparts, that presents a paradox. Resources are needed to innovate, but standing still may prove even more expensive. Amy believes publishers have to accept that reality: “The climate, ongoing changes and challenges that we’re all working through necessitate ongoing innovation. Either you take a leading role and innovate, or you’re just left behind.” Perhaps no initiative illustrates MIT Press’s willingness to challenge established publishing models more than Direct to Open. Launched in 2021 to make scholarly monographs openly available regardless of an author’s institutional funding, the programme has become one of the most closely watched experiments in academic publishing. title: Open GLAM as OER: Digital cultural heritage and the intersections of primary source literacy and information literacy
content: Abstract:  Many cultural heritage organizations, including galleries, libraries, archives, and museums (GLAM), are adopting open licensing policies for their digital collections, an approach known as Open GLAM. Open access allows these resources to be shared with broad audiences while open licensing permits these resources to be used as OER. This chapter examines the use of Open GLAM resources as OER and explores how the use of Open GLAM resources as OER connects with information literacy and, more specifically, primary source literacy. It also examines considerations for cultural heritage organizations that adapt Open GLAM policies and approaches. Students using Open GLAM collections must develop skills to search these resources, understand related copyright issues, and consider the ethics of using culturally sensitive materials.

content: Abstract: This article seeks to determine the extent to which the principle of persistence is observed by repositories and the organizations that operate them. In addition, the impact that negative repository persistence levels may be having on the scholarly record is assessed. This is achieved by interrogating and combining data on European repositories from several repository registries and web-scraped sources, including the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, which creates a unique dataset of historic repository locations and their OAI-PMH endpoints. Then, this data is used as the basis for text mining CORE, a vast corpus of scholarly outputs, to determine the extent to which impersistent European repository content has permeated the scholarly literature. The findings indicate that over one-fifth of European repositories (greater than 20 per cent) could be classified as “dead,” with an even greater proportion (greater than 40 per cent) of the machine interfaces associated with these repositories similarly dead. content: "Scholarly communication benefits from multiple pathways for evaluating research rather than relying exclusively on traditional journal-organized peer review. Across the open science ecosystem, organizations are experimenting with ways to separate the functions of publishing, reviewing, and curating research, broadening participation while reducing dependence on any single institution or gatekeeper. This broader vision is reflected in the growing Publish–Review–Curate (PRC) movement. PREreview is one example within this ecosystem. Our focus is on building open tools and cultivating communities that connect researchers seeking feedback with people willing to share their expertise. Other organizations are exploring complementary approaches. Review Commons coordinates expert peer review independently of journals before manuscript submission, allowing reviews to travel with the work across participating publishers. title: Intellectual Property as a Barrier to Science Communication under the Right to Science: Creating a Global Scholarly Knowledge Commons
content: Abstract: Is IP more a facilitator or barrier to science communication under the right to science, both within countries and across borders, including between the Global North and Global South? This chapter examines the effects of copyright in scientific publications on the diffusion of science and considers the effects of university patenting on knowledge transfer. It proposes addressing this question from a commons perspective. In particular, it argues that, under the right to science of international human rights law, scientific and technological knowledge produced with public funding should, as far as possible, be viewed as part of an intangible scholarly knowledge commons. This commons is crucial for further research and development and, in many respects, also constitutes a source of accessible benefits for citizens. IP rights should interfere with this commons only where absolutely necessary. The discussion enquires how the commons surrounding scientific publications and university inventions may be preserved and potentially expanded. title: Institutional Repositories
content: Abstract: Institutional Repositories manage and preserve an institution’s own content. Since their introduction over 25 years ago, Institutional Repositories have been established in universities and institutions around the world. Yet many people, even within the scholarly world, are unaware of the work that repositories carry out, and the essential role they play. Institutional Repositories is a much-needed guide to repositories, past and present. Written by a repository manager and trainer, this fully peer-reviewed book assumes no prior knowledge, and guides the reader through all the activities carried out by the repository team, including (but not limited to) ensuring green Open Access, and ensuring maximum impact for the institution’s research output, as well as providing a collective memory for the organization, often capturing content that would otherwise be lost. title: Manuscript Rejection on the Pretext of “Limited Space”: An Ethical and Economic Dilemma | Journal of Bioethical Inquiry | Springer Nature Link
content: Abstract: In the digital age, where physical space constraints in scholarly publishing have largely diminished, the recurring editorial justification of “limited space” for manuscript rejection appears increasingly indefensible. This commentary critically examines the ethical and economic dimensions of this rationale, particularly when it results in redirection to fee-based open access (OA) sister journals. While peer-reviewed publication decisions are ideally grounded in scientific merit, novelty, and methodological rigor, the authors argue that the space limitation rationale may function as a pretext to curate journal branding or steer submissions toward revenue-generating platforms. The expansion of OA publishing, though intended to democratize knowledge dissemination, has in some cases evolved into a profit-driven model that imposes article processing charges on authors. Such practices risk compromising editorial transparency, fairness, and academic equity. The authors advocate for clearer editorial policies, increased transparency in decision-making, and the adoption of mechanisms such as dynamic submission dashboards to inform authors of real-time publication capacity.

title: FRED enables standardized FAIR metadata generation and management for omics research | Scientific Reports
content: Abstract: Scientific research relies on transparent dissemination of data and its associated interpretations, including raw data, metadata, experimental design, and data processing details. Production and handling of research data represents an ongoing challenge, extending beyond publication into individual facilities, institutes and research groups, often termed Research Data Management (RDM). It is foundational to scientific discovery and aligned with the FAIR principles. Although the majority of peer-reviewed journals require raw data deposition in public repositories in alignment with FAIR principles, metadata frequently lacks standardization, hindering effective utilization and sharing of research findings. Here we present FRED, a generalized toolkit for FAIR metadata management in omics research based on a flexible, machine-readable YAML format. FRED enables (i) guided, dialog-based creation of metadata files, (ii) structured semantic validation, (iii) logical cross-file search, (iv) API-based integration with external systems, and (v) self-hosted web deployment. title: Open access, unequal access: why publication fee waivers still exclude many researchers | BMJ Global Health
content:
"Summary 


	
	Article processing charges (APCs) have moved the cost of publishing from institutions to individual researchers, creating new financial barriers for those without institutional or national support.
	
	
	World Bank income classification is widely used to determine APC waiver and discount eligibility but we argue that it is an unsuitable basis for publication-fee support.
	
	
	Researchers in some upper-middle-income and high-income countries with low research investment and structural vulnerability face barriers similar to those in low-income settings, but they remain excluded from waiver schemes.
	
	
	Journal editors, funders and policymakers should adopt multi-criterion eligibility, including research and development (R&D) expenditure, structural vulnerability, lead-researcher affiliation and authorship contribution verification and extend institutional Read-and-Publish agreements to under-resourced settings."

title: Doing Open Social Science | LSE Press
content: "Open science is a set of principles and practices that aims to make research from all fields accessible to everyone for the benefit of researchers and society as a whole. Doing Open Social Science: A Guide for Researchers is the first comprehensive book setting out the principles and practices of open research, tailored specifically for those in the social science disciplines, at every career stage, offering practical advice on how to make research more transparent, trustworthy and reusable. Divided into four parts, the book explores the core principles and philosophy of open social science. Part II addresses how to improve the reproducibility of research through open approaches, including chapters on the principles and tools of documenting research as you go and on open data practices. Part III focuses on open practices within the qualitative social sciences. Chapters examine interview-based research, case studies and fieldwork, systematic documentation analysis, archival data and the role of openness in citizen (social) science. Part IV addresses shifting research cultures, with chapters on strategies for presenting research clearly and accessibly to maximise reach and impact
